President’s Message
by Don Gamble
Welcome back everyone.
I hope your summer included at least a little time at the
lathe, because we’re heading into a full season of woodturn
ing, and there’s a lot to look forward to.
Thank you to everyone who came out to the Summer BBQ.
It was a terrific afternoon — great turnout, great conversa
tions — and it added about $905 to the Guild. Days like that
remind us why this Guild works: people show up, connect,
and enjoy being part of a community.
A couple of important updates as we start the season. With
KMS building a new warehouse and renting out part of the
current one, we were understandably concerned about the
future of our workshop space. While we don’t yet know the
long-term picture, we have been given the green light for the
Fall, and nothing is imminent that would change this. We’re
continuing to work closely with KMS and will keep everyone
informed.
On the tech side, we thought we were facing a full replace
ment of our vMix PC because it wasn’t Windows 11 compat
ible. A solution was found, and a new video card has given
the system a second life. Hopefully the picture is noticeably
sharper for anyone watching the demo on screen or via
Zoom — a small upgrade with a big impact.
Now, mark your calendars. Monthly meetings are Septem
ber 24, October 22, and November 26. Introduction to Bowl
Turning class runs October 3, 4, and 10, and the Introduction
to Spindle Turning class runs November 14 and 15 — five
seats each, so watch for registration.
And from October 24 to 26, we welcome Heather Marusiak,
a turner whose work has earned recognition at other guilds
and symposiums for her sculptural forms, bold surface
treatments, and her ability to teach both foundational and
advanced techniques with clarity and enthusiasm. Her
Saturday demo and Sunday/Monday workshops are open
for registration now.
Which brings me to what I really want to highlight.
Every visiting demonstrator’s Saturday demo has given me
something I didn’t expect — the offhand fix, the clever work
around, the small detail that quietly solves a problem I’ve
been stepping around. And the conversations in the room
matter just as much. You end the day knowing people you’d
only nodded at before.
So let’s make October 24 a full house. If you haven’t been to
a demonstrator day in a while — or ever — this is the one to
come to. It’s a full day of watching a professional artist work
at a level most of us only see online, close enough to see
exactly how a cut is made and to ask why it worked. No pres
sure to turn like a pro — just sit back, enjoy, watch, learn,
and talk woodturning with people who care about it as
much as you do. If you want hands-on time, the workshops
on Sunday and Monday are where that happens.
And here’s what I’d love everyone to do as we kick-off the
season. At our September meeting, make a point of arrang
ing to meet someone at one of these Saturday demos — or
be brave and use the online Member Directory to reconnect
with that person you had a great conversation with last year.
And while you’re there, now would be a great time to add
your picture to your profile so others can find you just as
easily. These Saturday demos are one of the best ways to
turn a quick chat into a real connection, and they’re a big
part of what makes this Guild feel alive and growing. Heath
er’s sessions have sold out at other guilds and symposiums,
and I’d like our room to feel just as full and just as engaged.
Let’s start the season strong. Let’s fill the room for Heather.
See you on the 25th.

Editor’s Notes
by Britchie
Hello everyone. And welcome back with the 250th edition of
our newsletter.
In this issue are two brand new segments, both of which
have been spearheaded by Pippa Lattey but will be open to
members to make their own contributions. The first, called
“Tools, Tech & Tips” (the ‘Tech’ could be for technology or
technique) is all about bought or custom-made tools, wid
gets, fixtures & jigs that offer woodturners innovative and/
or time-saving ways of making things. The second: “Books &
Publications” is where you will find references and reviews
of any turning related literature including books, magazine
articles, online media and links.
Our cover this month features a superbly finished Urn made
by Cathy Friesen at the request of her Aunt. Cathy has put
together an illustrated step-by-step account of how she
made the piece and some of the unexpected challenges she
encountered along the way.
Talking of challenges, Lucas Siba has penned a “things I
wished I’d known” style article based on his own experienc
es and lessons learned since starting out in wood turning.
Titled “Five Years of Shavings”, Lucas describes some the
traps he fell into and offers tips which I’m sure will resonate
with many members regardless of their skill level (the one
that tracks with me personally is #11).
Our Member Spotlight features Bob Gilson, widely known
as our videocam man and also our Guild’s Secretary. Bob
offers us a glimpse into his world producing and selling
turned wooden objects through various markets throughout
the summer, plus his life-changing connection with one
our craft’s most renowned figures which resulted in a new
approach as well as a new lathe.
We’ve a new type of tree highlighted in the ‘Know Your Spe
cies” segment written by Mike Moult. This month it’s Black
Locust—one of its authors favourite woods to work with.
Lastly, but not leastly, we’ve another great selection of mem
ber work in the Instant Gallery and President’s challenge
sections.
Happy turning!

15% Discount for GVWG Members
If you give the cashier your phone number, you will only get
the store 5% non-Guild discount. By saying GVWG instead you
get the 15% Guild discount.
If you are buying something that needs a warranty, just give
them your Name and Address and that will go on the electron
ic file. If the item you are buying has a flyer sale that is better
than the 15%, then you will automatically get the better rate.
Every purchase you make in the store by using this process
adds to our GVWG Credit account which we use to buy KMS
gift certificate prizes. We even bought our Laguna lathe for
Sapperton Hall with this! By doing this you are giving yourself
a better discount and helping the guild at the same time.
If you are an out-of-town Guild member, all you have to do is
type in GVWG as the customer name when buying, and type in
your full name, address etc. in the ‘ship-to’ field and you will
get the 15% discount.
The 15% is an average savings and is based on the cost mar
gins from that manufacturer. This does not apply to published
special flyer items. If we all do this, we can even get up to a
bigger discount level in future!

The Making of
Marg’s Urn 2026
by Cathy Friesen
Several years ago my aunt asked me to make her urn. She
asked that it not be a tall traditional looking urn. Making such
a personal piece for someone who is still alive requires careful
consideration and I struggled with options and ideas until I
saw Larry Stevenson’s demonstration of the quilting pattern. I
had a piece of spalted Maple that my dad (her brother) had cut
down years ago that I thought might do the trick.
My husband, Vic helped
work it into a more turn
able shape for me.
I turned and hollowed
the Maple base. It wasn’t
a very good piece of
wood for turning so I
wasn’t able to turn it
very thin. I made a pencil
holder that fit in the ban
jo and swiveled to mark
pencil lines to guide the
creation of a quilted
pattern on the body.
Next I had to make a lid that would fit the curve of the base.
I decided to use metal
threaded inserts to
connect the lid to the
base so I made sure the
opening was the right
size to fit. I placed the brass
threaded insert into the base
and went in for dinner. When
I came out the next morning
the base had changed shape
so much that I couldn’t get the
brass ring out. That was not a problem but I was sure glad
I had decided to use the metal threads (Link: https://www.
youtube.com/watch?v=TacGU8V1JQs).
Then I penciled-in the Inter-City Quilt Design on the base and
using my pyrography pen I burned in the design.
Now I had to decide what colour to make it. I used my
computer to try a
number of different
colours. I decided
on a violet and cop
per combination.
The goal was to
make it look some
what 3 dimensional.
Following Larry’s
instructions, I used
inks, acrylics and
interference paints
to give it a subtle shine. I painted the inside of the lid and
the inside of the urn to resemble the sky, looking up towards
Heaven. And left a spot on the bottom for the kids to have a
small plaque engraved with whatever they like.
See Larry Stevenson’s article “Layout of Geometric Designs”
featured in the March 2026 GVWG Newsletter.
Got a project you’d like to see featured in our front page?
Get in touch by email: editor@gvwg.ca

M E M B E R A R T I C L E
But clichés usually earn their keep. These articles are fun to
write, fun to read, and handy for the folks a few steps behind.
I’m not the first to write one and I won’t be the last. The twist
is that my list will look a little different from the ones before it,
because the turning world never sits still.
So five years in, here’s what I wish I’d known, or believed,
sooner.
1. You can’t buy your way to a clean cut. For my first couple
of years I was quietly certain that the next purchase (a better
gouge, a fancier grind, a tool with a longer name and a bigger
price tag) was the thing standing between me and the results
I wanted. It never was. The tool doesn’t turn the wood; you
do. A shelf full of gouges just buys you more ways to make the
same mistakes.
2. Sharpen far more often than feels reasonable. If you’re
wondering whether it’s getting dull, you waited too long. The
best mental shift I ever made was treating gouges like sandpa
per—consumables, not heirlooms. Once I stopped guarding
the steel and sharpened whenever the cut felt off, everything
got easier, and (bonus) the more I sharpened the better I got at
it, so I removed less metal each time.
3. Nobody warns you about CBN wheels. When you finally
upgrade to a CBN wheel—and you will— two things caught me
off guard. First, a brand-new wheel is hungry. Those first few
grinds are far more aggressive than you’d expect, and it’ll strip
steel fast enough to make you flinch. Don’t panic, and don’t
assume you bought the wrong grit; after a few sharpenings it
settles right down into the wheel you actually paid for. Second,
and this one took me embarrassingly long to learn, hang a
wire brush right next to the grinder. I spent ages deep-cleaning
gunked-up wheels before I clued in. One or two quick strokes
between sharpenings clears the pitch, keeps the wheel cutting
clean, and makes a real difference.
4. Stop chasing the perfect grind. Early on I fell hard down
the grind rabbit hole — 40/40, swept-back, this jig, that angle,
forever wondering how each one would feel. It’s fascinating
stuff, and I regret to report I became a serial re-grinder, but
here’s what I wish I’d absorbed sooner: every time you reshape
a tool, you grind away a chunk of steel you can’t get back. If
you know you’re a gouge tinkerer, do your experimenting on
plain HSS, not M42 Cryo. But the real secret is that no angle on
earth beats hours with the tool in your hands, actually cutting
wood. Mileage makes the turner, not the grind.
5. The secondary bevel is easier than it sounds. Learn it early.
New turners hear “put a secondary bevel on your bowl gouge”
and picture some fiddly advanced-class wizardry. It isn’t. A few
extra strokes and one small adjustment on the grinder, and
there it is. And on the inside curve of a bowl, where tool marks
love to hide, that little second bevel lets you follow the wall
cleanly and leave a far tidier surface. Tiny investment, dispro
portionate payoff. I wish I’d stopped being intimidated by it
years earlier.
6. Say your ABC’s every single cut: Anchor, Bevel, Cut. Anchor
the tool on the rest, rub the bevel, then start cutting. Direct
your pressure down onto the toolrest, not into the wood —
beginners (hello) shove the tool at the spinning blank and
wonder where the catch came from. Learn to glide the bevel
and let the tool do the cutting. And yes, move the toolrest in
nice and close, after you’ve turned the lathe off.
7. Making the same thing twice is the real test. Most turners
can walk up to a blank and let a shape emerge. That’s how I
spent most of my first few years. However, turning a second
piece to match the first (same dimensions, same curve, same
fit) is one of the hardest things in this craft, and it humbled me
in a hurry. It forces you to plan your cuts instead of discovering
Five Years
of Shavings
by Lucas Siba
Somewhere around the five (or ten) year
mark a lot of us hit the same milestone: we
sit down and write one of these. The lookback article. The “things I wish I’d known”
reflection. I’ve come to suspect that writ
ing one is a quiet rite of passage, proof to
yourself that you’ve been at it long enough
to have opinions worth inflicting on other
people.
(Continues on the next page)

M E M B E R A R T I C L E
them. If you want to fast-track your control and your eye, set
yourself the challenge: turn a matched pair, then a set of four.
Even small practice pieces will teach you more about deliber
ate shaping than a dozen one-off bowls.
8. Turn small, and turn firewood. Those bowls in the videos
are smaller than they look—often no bigger than six inches.
Make a dozen little ones and learn the moves before you go
big. And please don’t sacrifice your one gorgeous burl on the
altar of practice; the firewood pile is free and forgiving. If a
piece of wood is too beautiful to risk, do future-you a favour
and set it aside until your skills have caught up to it.
9. Green wood has opinions and it changes its mind after
you’ve gone to bed. My early bowls kept splitting overnight
and I took it personally. The lesson, learned the hard way and
often enough that I’ve probably lost more wood to cracking
than anyone in this guild, is that speed is the enemy: wood
cracks when moisture leaves it too fast. Rough-turn green
bowls to a roughly even wall, about a tenth of the diameter,
get the pith out, and then let the blank dry slow and steady
before you finish it. And don’t be fooled by a surface that feels
dry to the touch; dry on the outside almost never means dry
all the way through.
10. Slow down when you sand and never, ever skip a grit.
For two years I sanded too fast and hopscotched from coarse
to fine, then wondered why scratches “appeared” the moment
the finish went on. Heat is one of the culprits: high speed just
burnishes and can even crack the wood, and it destroys sand
paper. Slower actually cuts faster. Finer grits don’t erase coarse
scratches; they only hide them, so work through every grit,
clean the piece between them, check under an angled light,
and throw out worn paper. Sandpaper is a cutting tool.
11. Finishing is a skill, not a coat you slap on at the end. It
took me far too long to give finishing the same respect as ev
erything upstream of it. Every finish—oil, varnish, lacquer, poly
urethane, the whole shelf, is really just another tool with its
own rules. Read the back of the bottle. Test it on offcuts. Learn
how it behaves in your shop, because your temperature and
humidity change everything about how it cures. There’s no
sadder sight than a beautifully turned form wearing a rushed,
blotchy finish. Give the last step the practice and patience you
gave the first ones.
12. Get in the room and ask everything. A good half-day with
a mentor or a club demo will short-circuit months of solo frus
tration; there’s simply no video substitute for watching a real
person’s stance, grip, and (best of all) how they recover when a
cut goes wrong. And once you’re in the room, ask. Every guild
I’ve come across (the AAW, ours, all of them) runs on the same
generous rule: there’s no such thing as a dumb question, and
most turners are genuinely delighted to be asked “how did
you do that?” Fair warning, though: ask two turners the same
question and you’ll come away with three answers. Outside of
the safety fundamentals, which we all respect, so much of this
craft (which tool you reach for, how you shape a curve, what
order you finish in) comes down to personal preference. Those
competing answers aren’t contradictions; they’re a menu.
Collect them, try them, and slowly build an approach that’s
your own.
13. Look after the turner, not just the turning. Wear the
face shield and the respirator — your eyes and lungs don’t
grow back. Take the five-minute break; it beats six months of
nursing a repetitive-strain injury. And never get cocky around a
spinning chunk of wood — kinetic energy respects neither rank
nor experience.
None of this came from a single breakthrough; it came from
a hundred small realizations, most of which showed up years
later than they should have. The mistakes were the best
teachers I had. The trick I eventually learned is to embrace the
fumble, figure out what went wrong, and try again.
And this list is nowhere near finished. The turning world keeps
moving, I keep finding fresh and more interesting ways to mess
up, and five years from now I’ll surely have a whole new batch
of things I wish I’d known today. If even one of these spares
you a cracked bowl, a gunky CBN wheel, or a drawer full of
tools you never needed, then this particular cliché will have
done its job.
Happy Turning, and may your bevels always be rubbing.
(Continued from the previous page)

YOUR PERSONAL SAFETY
Always wear Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) such as
approved safety glasses or goggles that include side protec
tors. Use a full face shield for larger bowl, vessel, or any turning
involving chucks and faceplates. Wear a dust mask or an air
filtration helmet in conjunction with proper ventilation and/
or a dust collection system as appropriate. Remember—it’s
the fine airborne particles that are harmful to your respiratory
system. Wear hearing protection during extended periods of
turning.
Tie back long hair and avoid long sleeves or loose clothing.
Remove rings and other jewelry, or any dangling objects that
may catch on rotating parts or accessories.
Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close attention to
unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop the lathe to investigate the
cause. Don’t operate machines when you are tired or under
the influence of drugs or alcohol.
WORKING SAFELY WITH YOUR LATHE
Ensure your workpiece is securely fastened. When using a
faceplate, be certain the workpiece is solidly mounted with
stout screws (#10 or #12 sheet metal screws as a minimum).
Do not use drywall or deck screws. When turning between
centers, check the workpiece is firmly mounted between the
headstock and tailstock and rotate your workpiece forwards/
backwards by hand to make sure it clears the toolrest and bed
before turning the lathe on.
Check all locking devices on the tailstock and tool rest as
sembly (rest and base) are tight before operating the lathe.
Check the speed of your lathe BEFORE turning it on. Use
slower speeds for larger diameters or rough pieces and higher
speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced.
Always start a piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is
balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the speed.
If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the machine to under
stand why. As a starting point, consult your operator’s manual
for recommended speeds for a particular lathe. Ensure the
lathe speed is compatible with the diameter of the blank.
Stay clear of danger zones directly behind and in front of the
workpiece. They are the most likely areas for a piece to travel
as it comes off the lathe. A good safety habit is to step out of
this zone when turning on the lathe, keeping your hand on the
switch in case you need to turn the machine off. When observ
ing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
Turn the lathe off before adjusting anything including the
tool rest or tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches, and knock
out bars immediately after use. Never leave them in place,
even for a moment. Always remove the tool rest before sand
ing, finishing, or polishing operations.
Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced
woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and proce
dures not recommended for beginning turners.
Exercise extra caution when using stock with cracks, splits,
checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular shapes or protuberanc
es. Beginners should avoid these types of stock until they have
greater knowledge of working such wood.
Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding the tool
in a controlled but comfortable manner. Always contact the
tool rest with the tool before contacting the wood.
Never work with a lathe in reverse unless the chuck is using
a locking set-screw. It is possible for a chuck or faceplate to
unscrew unless it is fitted securely on the lathe spindle.
Don’t overreach. Keep proper footing and keep your balance

S A F E T Y G U I D E L I N E S
(Continues on the next page)
You mostly work on your own so safety is
YOUR responsibility. Please take the time to
read our safety guidelines and make them part
of your daily turning practice. Be safe out there!

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | S E P T E M B E R 2 0 2 6
at all times.
Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer performance.
Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool for a purpose for which
it was not designed or intended.
Consider your work environment. Don’t use a lathe in damp
or wet locations. Do not use in presence of flammable liquids
or gases, and always keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher
close at hand. Keep your work area well lit.
Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric cords for dam
age. Avoid the use of extension cords.
Never leave a lathe running unattended. Turn power off.
Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a complete stop.
SAFETY MAINTENANCE
Keep your lathe in good repair. Ensure belt guards or protec
tive covers are in place. Check for damaged parts, alignment,
binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect
its operation.
Read and follow safety guidelines for your lathe and other
workshop equipment. Many accidents to woodturners occur
while using saws, especially bandsaws and chainsaws.

M E M B E R S P O T L I G H T
30 years ago a friend gifted me a small General lathe. My
first grandchild was about to be born so I decided to make a
cradle.
The design I chose had four turned spindles for the four cor
ners of the box bracketing the head and foot boards and a set
of smaller spindles for each side panel. The training I received
in high school paid off and muscle memory allowed a really
enjoyable process and a beautiful piece to present to my son
and daughter-in-law for their first born. I was hooked right
from the get go and as life would have it my daughter followed
suit with my son-in-law and I had to make a second cradle.
Using the same basic design the second was enhanced by
carved head and foot boards. I knew then I wanted to become
a wood turner.
My workshop is a 60’ by 20’ room in the parkade within the
housing Co-op my wife and I live in. I share the space with a
couple others but I am the only woodturner in the group. I am
fortunate to have a Robust American Beauty as my main lathe
that I bought from David Ellsworth in 2018.
Bob Gilson
with Diana Dougherty

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | S E P T E M B E R 2 0 2 6
The tools I like to use the most at my lathe are my bowl goug
es, skews and spindle gouges. I really like to use my vacuum
chuck as well because it’s such a time saver.
My favourite wood is figured Maple but Walnut and Cherry are
close behind. Truthfully though, I just love wood in general.
My preferred finishes are a mineral oil and beeswax mix for util
ity pieces and wipe-on-poly for most everything else although
sometimes I really like just burnishing a piece with shavings
and leaving it like that.
I like doing flat work sometimes at Christmas for family gifts.
I have a scroll saw and a bandsaw and I like to make boxes
and ornaments. I also like to do relief carving and sculpting. I
am inspired by nature and the trees that provide me with the
material I use to create with.
Without a doubt David Ellsworth has had the greatest influ
ence on my development as a turner. He introduced me to the
joy of turning green wood and all of the magic that unfolds as
a piece changes shape in its finishing. He taught me to let the
wood speak and determine what it wants to be.
My wife makes jackets and hats and I make bowls, boxes and
hollow forms and we sell our creations at farmers markets in
the lower mainland and the gulf islands throughout the sum
mer and at Christmas. This summer we attended the Ladner
Village Market, the Southlands Market and the Galiano Island
Market.
The most challenging piece that I have made so far is a work
in progress still. Its a large hollow form vessel made from a
Galiano Island cherry tree root.
My favourite project to-date has been exploring offset turning
forms, but I have also really enjoyed the time I’ve spent with
the Doctor aka Art Liestman, learning techniques to texture
and colour wood and exploring design. Art has been a true
inspiration.
I see my work
moving toward
larger pieces and
irregular shaped
hollow forms
with textured and
coloured com
ponents. I would
really like to try
sandblasting one
of these days.
David Ellsworth told me straight up that when I got home
from the time spent with him that I should join my local Guild.
I did and now I am a proud member and part of the board and
the AV team. I look forward to encouraging other potential
members as David encouraged me with such good advice.

AV Technology Updated
by Brian Lunt
The team got together over the summer and created a num
ber of positive changes. First we have to thank Don Gamble
for applying his computer savvy and forcing our old mother
board into accepting Windows 11 and installing a dedicated
graphics card. This saved us the expense of buying a new
desktop computer.
As a result, we were able to attach the guild monitor, Sap
perton Hall TV and Demonstrator monitor all onto their own
dedicated powered graphic ports. This improved image res
olution and enabled the demonstrator monitor to now show
a mirror image so the demonstrator does not have to guess
anymore where the camera image is coming from.
Also with this upgrade, we were able to move all our camera
inputs to their own dedicated USB ports that will further
increase image quality. This eliminated a data pinch point
that we had previously where all the cameras were feeding
into one USB power bar.
We reviewed and streamlined procedures to make it easier
for the AV Team to create the experience of woodturning to
members in the hall and to fellow turners on Zoom.
If you are interested in the AV Team and would like to volun
teer, just come visit us and see what we are doing.

Black Locust is a species
originally native to the South
Eastern United States. It now
grows across North America
and has been propagated
worldwide. In Canada it is
found in Ontario, East to Nova
Scotia and in British Colum
bia. Contrary to popular be
lief, it is not related to Acacia
trees which are tropical and
grow in Africa and Australia.
The tree is desirable because of several characteristics. The
wood is hard and strong (Janka hardness 1700). The timber is
durable and very rot resistant. Fence posts made from black
locust outlast treated timber by several times. The wood is an
exceptional fuel as it has a very high BTU. The flowers produce
fine honey.
Black Locust is now consid
ered invasive almost world
wide. It grows rapidly and
spreads through suckers and
seeds. Once cut down it will
sprout back with multiple
shoots (this is one of the rea
sons it was planted as it gives
a continuous supply of fence
posts through the practice of
coppicing). This makes it diffi
cult to eradicate. In order to eradicate the tree must be ground
down and herbicide applied to the roots. This may have to be
repeated for several years.
Black Locust is reported to be toxic. Bark, shoots, seed pods
and seeds are especially so while the flowers are considered
non-toxic. Livestock, especial horses, will eat the bark off fence
posts and trees making them ill. Continued exposure my be
fatal to livestock. There are very few case reports of human
toxic reactions to Black Locust exposure. Dust has been report
ed to cause skin and eye irritation and less commonly nausea.
Proper PPE should be used when working with it.
The wood usually has a straight grain with medium figure. It
machines well despite being very hard and stiff and tends to
dull tools because
of its hardness. It
is a good wood
for turning, easy
to work despite its
hardness.
Of special note, the
sapwood is pale
and the heartwood
greenish golden to brown in colour which can give distinct
patterns. The heartwood is high in tannins so when it’s fumed
with ammonia will turn a rich black while the sapwood retains
its pale colour.

Improvised Shop Tools
by Pippa Lattey
Looking around my studio, I am amused to see quite a few
handmade and personalized tools. Each tool is made quickly,
with materials I have on hand. I make a tool when inspiration
hits. Sometimes I have what I think is a brilliant idea to solve a
technical problem. Sometimes I am fed up with struggling to
do something. Always, the tool is made rapidly, in a flurry of
energy, so I can get on with my “real” project.
I am interested in tools as cultural objects, design objects, and
as extensions of our selves: we develop intimate, personal
connections with our tools. I love tools as objects because
they are used. They develop patina, nicks, and cracks from
use. They are beautiful.
All this to say, I would like to share a few of my own quirky,
personalized and improvised tools. I also invite GVWG mem
bers to share their own Improvised Implements: tools, fixtures,
shop furniture, etc. Send in a photo or two and a short story
about your tool: How it was made? How much time or thought
went into it? What prompted you to make it? How do you
actually use it?
1. Knob Turner
This tool is for adjusting the
Blade Guides on my Rikon
Bandsaw. The guides are
plastic knobs that must be
quite tight, but my fingers are
not strong enough, especially
in tight spaces. It’s made of
an offcut of Birch, from the
very first log that I milled on
my new bandsaw. I added a
rare earth magnet to keep in
on the side of the bandsaw.
2. Wax stick
This is a candle with a rare earth magnet, stuck to the side of
my bandsaw. When cutting very green wood, I periodically
“wax” the blade by rubbing the candle on it, while the saw
is running. This helps prevent the blade from gumming up,
saving me from the time-consuming job of cleaning the goo
off the bandsaw blade and tires.
3. Depth Drill
This is a tool I have been mean
ing to make for years. I have
seen several demonstrators use
them, to establish a depth be
fore hollowing a bowl, box, etc.
I was finally motivated to make
one this August, while making
small cups / hollow forms.
The tool is a quarter inch drill
bit in a turned handle. I did not
glue it in, as I was in a hurry to
get back to turning. After a few
uses, the bit became loose. So,
I fixed it the
next time I
had some 5
minute epoxy
out (which
happened to
be tinted pink
to decorate
some repaired
cracks). There
is no finish on the wood, and you can see where my messy
gloves smeared pigment on the handle.
4. Bench Hook
As you can see, my
Bench Hook is well
used. I made it from
offcuts a year or two
ago. This is techni
cally not a tool, but
a fixture, used to
secure a piece while
working on it. It sits
on a table or bench,
and provides a block to push against while carving with chis
els, gouges, etc. Mine has a V notch to fit turned objects. I first
used a Bench Hook when carving linoleum and wood blocks
for printmaking. I often use it to carve the nub off the bottom
of small dishes, and for hand carving details.

Oneway Paint Mixer
by Ed Pretty
This all started a couple of months ago when Mike Moster
messaged me about a slick way of mixing rattle can paints to
avoid the seemingly endless and probably ineffective shaking
prior to spraying. I think we’ve all given it the old college try
then said to hell with it about 45 seconds into the effort. Mike
sent a video of a PVC tube mounted on a hand drill that spun
the can, mixing in no time flat.
Great idea! Gonna make one! Cue: procrastination. I already
had the stuff I needed but it all sat on the shelf until I needed
to use some rattle can lacquer, whereupon I kicked my butt
for not assembling the goods. I was in a hurry, only needing
to turn one part but thought, “Hey! Mount it in the lathe!” It
seemed to work after I adjusted the speed so that I could hear
the marble clunking in the can. A couple minutes while prep
ping the piece to be sprayed and I was in business.
Fast forward to yesterday when I needed to use some polyure
thane that had sat on the shelf for at least three years. I was
confident that it would be OK because I had put a finish on
exactly one plane handle then put it on the shelf. At the time,
the only issue was that it was supposed to be satin, but the
plane handle shone like the sun, so clearly even when new,
the solids that determines the level of the sheen had already
settled in the can.
I opened the can and sure enough it looked new, but when I
dug down with a little stir stick there was a layer of goo on the
bottom that was as thick as tar. I tried dragging it back and
forth to cut it into pieces and that sort of worked but clearly, I
was getting nowhere. Light bulb moment! Rattle can!
I dropped a couple of ½” nuts in the can, sealed it up, mount
ed it in the lathe between centers, then adjusted the speed
so I could hear the nuts clanking away in the can. Off to other
chores for an hour or so then back for a quick check. I could
hear sloshing instead of clanking so opened it up and… ta da!
A stir stick across the bottom confirmed that the sludge layer
was gone. Not only that, the mixture definitely had the hazy
look of a satin finish. Those two nuts live in that can now. I
know that some of you may not have a chuck big enough to
grab a one liter paint can but there’s no problem turning a disk
to fit of the bottom (or top) of the can jam chuck style. Even if
you have a chuck that fits the can, I think the tailstock holding
things in place is pretty good insurance against refinishing your
lathe and whole shop interior. Not everyone will have a su
per-duper cone for their live center, but I know a piece of wood
between the can and live center would do the trick. I used
pretty much that set up for the rattle can mixer using a smaller
chuck and a small block of wood against the plastic top.
I found that about 200 rpm did the trick in my case. A low
speed like 200 rpm over an extended time could cause your
motor or motor control to dangerously overheat. If you have
a direct drive (i.e. Nova) that’s not a problem but if you have
multiple ranges on your lathe (mine has three steps), I think
it’s good idea to use the low range so that your motor will be
going as fast as possible at the low output speed.
Using the jam chuck approach, I can see this working even for
a 4-liter can, but I think a 20-liter pail is a bit of a stretch. But
then…

T H E C I R C U L A R | G R E AT E R V A N C O U V E R W O O D T U R N E R S G U I L D | S E P T E M B E R 2 0 2 6
The Hidden Life of Trees explains how trees live, grow
and breath. It is also an expose on the social lives of
trees. Yes, trees have fascinating social networks. They
develop friendly relationships, even between tree spe
cies, and between trees and birds, bugs, and funghi.
Descriptions of tree growth are a pleasure to read, es
pecially for a woodturner who knows a little about the
structure of wood. The language is descriptive, never
technical. Wohlleben uses the metaphor of bark as skin
to explain how bark grows, creases, sheds, and protects
the tree from disease and damage. This metaphor helps
to understand the structure of the tree, but it also helps
us to relate to the tree. We are alike, because we both
have skin!
The book is filled with many short chapters including
tree communication, aging, water, light and air. My
favourite chapter is about urban trees, titled “Street
Kids”. Trees planted in parks and lining streets grow
up as solitary creatures, without nearby relatives to
provide support. They are less healthy, and ultimately
they have shorter lives than if they grew up in a forest,
surrounded by a community of trees. Wohlleben refers
to the healthy forest as a kindergarten for young trees,
growing up in the care of much older trees.
The Hidden Life of Trees was first published in German
in 2015, well before our local Susanne Simard’s book
Finding the Mother Tree (2021). Wohlleben was familiar
with Simard’s ideas about maternal instincts in trees,
and her research on communication between roots
and mycorrhizal fungi: what she called the “Wood Wide
Web”. Like Simard, Wohlleben has spent his life working
with forests.
The book will make you think differently about trees.
When you walk in a park or forest you will notice tree
health, and you will appreciate the quirks of the Maple,
the Douglas Fir, and the Oak.
